summary: MACGen is a four-role pipeline for secure code generation: a Planner, a Security Advisor (early-exit triage, CWE inference, RAG over a CERT/OWASP guideline KB, code-based guideline synthesis), a Code Generator, and a Reviewer. Agents exchange only structured artifacts, not the shared dialogue. Evaluated on CWEval (119 tasks, 5 languages, 6 LLMs) and BaxBench (392 tasks, 6 backend languages, 4 LLMs), it reports the best joint functional-and-secure pass rate (F&S@1) against four published inference-time baselines.

claims.claim: MACGen improves F&S@1 over direct prompting by 19.61pp on CWEval on average across six LLMs, reaching up to 70.59%.
claims.evidence: Table 1 (CWEval, 119 tasks) Δ columns. The 70.59 figure appears repeatedly in the table. Each cell comes from a single temperature-0 run with no variance. Table 7 (k=3, temp 0.5) preserves the ranking for GPT-4o.

claims.claim: On BaxBench MACGen improves F&S@1 by 10.57pp on average and achieves the best F&S@1.
claims.evidence: Table 2: GPT-4o 21.17→31.12 (+9.95) and GPT-4o-mini 10.76→21.94 (+11.18), so 10.57 is the mean of those two models only. Table 2 also has GPT-5.1 (35.71→51.53) and Claude Sonnet 5 (42.35→61.22). Over INDICT the margins are small: 31.12 vs 30.36, 51.53 vs 48.47, 61.22 vs 59.69, with INDICT ahead on Func@1 for GPT-5.1 (66.07 vs 62.50). These are single runs with no CIs, so the advantage over INDICT is within plausible noise.

claims.claim: Artifact-only interfaces beat a shared-context variant: +20.17% on CWEval with GPT-4o-mini and +8.67% on BaxBench with GPT-4o.
claims.evidence: Figure 5 plus Appendix I. This is an internal ablation against MACGen-Shared, which gets full upstream scratchpads. It is a reasonable controlled comparison but has no variance.

claims.claim: MACGen uses 16% of INDICT's tokens and costs about the same as RAG baselines.
claims.evidence: Table 3: 220,916 vs 1,411,754 total tokens, $0.91 vs $4.68. Measured on only 25 Python CWEval tasks with GPT-4o. RESCUE is cheaper ($0.23, 43,641 tokens).

claims.claim: Each agent and each Security Advisor component contributes.
claims.evidence: Tables 4–5 ablations show F&S@1 dropping when any agent or component is removed, on a subset of models. Single runs.

patterns.note: A role-specialized four-agent pipeline beats single-pass prompting and RAG baselines on two secure-code benchmarks. Its margin over the shared-dialogue multi-agent baseline INDICT is small.
Planner-first then coder. Removing the Planner reduces F&S@1 in Table 4.

Passing only compact upstream artifacts instead of full dialogue improves F&S@1 over the MACGen-Shared variant (Fig. 5) and cuts tokens (Table 3). This is an alternative to compacting a context after it has grown.
An LLM Reviewer checks functionality and security against the guidelines. The final judge is the benchmark oracles, not the reviewer, and the reviewer's accuracy is never measured on its own.
Embedding retrieval over a normalized CERT/OWASP guideline KB. Removing standards-driven generation degrades F&S@1 (Table 5).
Only a syntax checker is in the loop. The Limitations section names static analyzers and pentest tooling as future work, so there is no SAST feedback.
Reports tokens, cost and latency (Table 3), and caps refinement at M=2 iterations.

methodology.sample: CWEval: 119 tasks. BaxBench: 392 tasks (28 scenarios × 14 frameworks). Plus HumanEval/HumanEval+ and LLMSecEval (150 tasks) in the appendices. Cost analysis on 25 Python tasks only.
methodology.baselines: Direct prompting, SecGuide, CodeGuarder, RESCUE (RAG-based) and INDICT (multi-agent). Baselines run with the hyperparameters from their original papers, and RESCUE with the official implementation. These are current and reasonably faithful, though not re-tuned per model.
methodology.models: CWEval: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5-Flash, Gemini 2.5-Flash-Lite, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, Qwen3-8B. BaxBench: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.1, Claude Sonnet 5.
methodology.variance: Temperature 0.0 single runs for the main tables. No seeds, SDs or CIs. Table 7 adds a pass@3 at temp 0.5 rather than repeated pass@1.
methodology.ablations: Agent ablation (Table 4), Security Advisor component ablation (Table 5), shared-context variant (Fig. 5), CWE group count C (App. F), sampling k (Table 7).
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed. CWEval and BaxBench are public, and the KB includes OWASP cheat sheets that may overlap benchmark exploit categories.
methodology.languages: C, C++, Python, JavaScript, Go (CWEval); Go, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust (BaxBench). No Java.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint. The comment says '8 pages' with no venue.
standards.artifacts: The paper states that all source code, evaluation logs and prompts are at github.com/Mishuni/macgen-secure-code. The ethics section says 'plan to release', which is slightly inconsistent.

biases.detail: Main results are single temperature-0 runs. The MACGen-vs-INDICT gaps on BaxBench (0.76–3.57pp) have no uncertainty estimate.
The authors built MACGen and selected the configuration (C=3/C=2, M=2). Baselines use default settings from their papers. The benchmark oracles are third-party, which mitigates this.
Cost is reported only for 25 Python tasks with GPT-4o, not on BaxBench, where the multi-file backends dominate.

The abstract's BaxBench '10.57pp average' covers only GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, while Table 2 also contains GPT-5.1 and Claude Sonnet 5. The intro says BaxBench was evaluated with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. The reporting is inconsistent, though the omitted models also improve.
Public benchmarks plus a KB built from OWASP/CERT material that overlaps the benchmarks' CWE targets. Not discussed.

verdict_reason: The abstract numbers are reproduced in Tables 1–2. Baselines are current, and evaluation covers 6 models on CWEval and 4 on BaxBench across 5–6 languages, with useful ablations. However, everything is a single deterministic run, the margin over INDICT is within likely noise, cost is measured on 25 Python tasks only, and Java is absent.
applicability: Moderately useful as a design pattern rather than a drop-in tool. The artifact-only handoff fits mixed agent hosts well: each stage (plan, security guidelines, code, review) writes a structured file instead of sharing a chat transcript, so stages can run on different hosts and be checked into the spec-driven workflow, and the plan doubles as a spec. For healthcare-education ingestion services, a 'security advisor' step that derives task-specific CWE guidance (input validation on ingested content, path handling, auth on delivery APIs) before coding is cheap (about $0.91 per 25 tasks on GPT-4o) and could live in one shared prompt/skill used across the ≥4 ingestion repos. Caveats: the paper has no Java/Spring evidence, and its reviewer is an LLM with no SAST in the loop. The team should pair this with Semgrep/Sonar rather than trust an LLM reviewer, and treat the gains as unproven for Java.
